If found, please return to Oliver Lyonbrooke.
Same reward as last time. (Still modest.)

CHULT

Book II

the journal of Oliver Lyonbrooke, continued

begun again in Omu, on stolen paper

STILL PRIVATE.
Yes, Luth. Still.

Still noted.
— L.

A word first

My first book is full. I wrote the last pages small and then I wrote in the margins, and then there were no margins left.

For days after that I had nothing to write on. I kept it all in my head, which is a terrible place to keep things.

This paper is Thayan, and so are the ink and the quills; I took them off the Red Wizards, and you will read how.

So the next pages are written afterwards, all at once, by lantern light.

I'll tell it in order. I promise I won't skip ahead to the good part, even though there is a very good part.

THREE DAYS OLLI WENT WITHOUT A BOOK. HE TOLD US ALL ALOUD INSTEAD. FIND HIM PAPER.

9 Mirtul · the palace ruins

Where we stood: under the palace of Omu, Vaeril's two friends are held by the yuan-ti. Down there, too, is one of the nine cubes, and Ras Nsi, the yuan-ti lord, who has it. And Zagmira, the Red Wizard with the two halves of a face, wants us to go and get it, together.

We don't trust her, and we went anyway.

She gave us a companion, Yamoch, called "the Shadow": very quick, with two eyes that move independently, and the unsettling habit of hearing and seeing everything.

HE WALKS BEHIND US. I LIKE NOT THAT WHICH WALKS BEHIND US.

We went round to the south side of the palace and looked for a way in. Vaeril found it: under the palms, behind a wall of thorn bushes, a narrow cave mouth going down into the earth. A few steps in, the cave stopped being a cave and became a passage somebody had cut.

Then back to the Red Wizards, to be made invisible. Ofar asked for darkvision as well, and didn't get it.

Then they made us invisible, and we went into the tunnel.

It is a very strange thing, being invisible in the dark. You walk, and you can't see the walls, and you can't see your feet, and you can't see your friends, and then you start to wonder if you are still there at all.

Ofar asked if he was still invisible.

If you can't see your hands, then yes. — L.
INVISIBLE AND BLIND. FOR A PALADIN, NO PLAN AT ALL. IT WORKED NONETHELESS.

At the bottom of the tunnel: a little lake under the rock, black water, low stalactites, and two rowboats pulled up on the stones. Each had a cowbell on the bow.

Nobody hangs a cowbell on a boat unless he wants to know when it moves, so we left the boats alone.

After the lake came the first carved serpents, where the walls stop being rock and start being yuan-ti, and we crept in.

A storeroom, and in the middle of it, coiled up like a bored quartermaster, a giant python.

It could hear us without seeing us, and it took that very badly.

So I deposited a ritual dagger with the dumb storage python: you hand it something, it counts it, and it calms down. I know this kind of snake; every warehouse in Baldur's Gate has a clerk exactly like it.

THE SNAKE IS CALM. THE DAGGER FROM THE SHRINE IS GONE. GOOD. NEVER DID I LIKE THAT DAGGER.

9 Mirtul · still under the palace

We needed the dungeon, where the prisoners are. The python knows everything in this place, so we tried to trick it.

We tried two stories on it. Ofar played a prisoner who had got out and wanted more bread for the others, and I played a guard who wanted to round the others up again.

Ofar won.

We still don't know where the dungeon is. Buuut we have bread!

OLLI PLAYS A GUARD WHO SAYS PLEASE. NO ONE BELIEVES A GUARD WHO SAYS PLEASE.

So we turned round and went into the big room with the blood fountain.

Five stone serpents hold up a balcony, and blood runs out of their mouths into a basin, and from the basin into a trough. I drew it small; it is anything but.

A whole troop of yuan-ti went past us, on their way to what Ofar calls the snake hole. We stood very still and very invisible.

Luth looked through a grate into the yuan-ti harem, and although I have asked him twice, he has not described it to me.

Then Salida came in. Salida from the ship: the stories at night, the serpent god, the hammock. The last time I saw her she was in a boat full of fresh adventurers. Now she had a tabaxi prisoner with her, and she whipped him across the room.

I knew she was fishy.

I didn't write that down at the time; being a gentleman, I wrote "what a woman" instead, and both halves of that were a mistake.

An actress. She poisoned herself to fool us, back then. I crossed her name out. — L.

Through the door she'd come from we saw a throne room, and an execution: a pureblood yuan-ti, still talking, still making a speech, until a much bigger one took his head off. Ofar says the big one was Ras Nsi himself.

In the main hall they were leading a prisoner away: an owlin, a woman.

Vaeril flew over, invisible, and dimension-doored her out of there as easily as lifting a cup off a table, and when he came back he knew the way to the dungeon.

ONE MINUTE WITH A PRISONER, AND HE HAS THE WAY. EITHER SHE SPEAKS FAST, OR SHE KNEW HIM.

Yamoch fetched his informant from the harem, Ishmakahl. The cube, she said, might be in the bedchamber behind the throne.

So we went towards the throne room to kill. Ras Nsi, the yuan-ti lord, has wanted all of Chult for longer than I have been alive, and it was time somebody told him no.

A fireball first, into a great many yuan-ti; and then it was Ofar and Ras Nsi, and for a while nobody else in the world.

Ofar killed Ras Nsi.

And at the end, the alarm, and Yamoch turned on us and became

the invisible son of a bitch.

9 Mirtul · night · the throne room

Then the gong, and yuan-ti coming down the long passage from the main hall, more of them every minute, and Yamoch somewhere in the room, invisible and on the other side now.

And then something knocked on the throne room from the other side, through the wide opening to the flooded cave. With its heads.

Ras Nsi's hydra.

We had been loud. Luckily it was also, just, too fat for the opening, a small door for a hydra that had eaten well, and that is the only reason I am writing this: it stayed wedged in the doorway and bit at whatever moved, and we moved a great deal.

THE SNAKE KING DEAD UPON HIS FLOOR. HIS HYDRA IN THE DOOR. HIS PEOPLE IN THE HALL. NONE WILL BE FIRST. GOOD. I WAIT.

In between bites we did what you do in the throne room of a dead snake king. We looted it.

And behind the throne I found the secret passage, because a throne like that always has one; as far as I can tell, that is what thrones are for.

Behind it: Ras Nsi's own rooms, and his things. Among them, a ruby with an eye inside it.

The eye follows me, and it is rotten, and I like it very much, which says something about me I'd rather not know.

Fancy. — L.

And I found the cube.

Luth went after Yamoch alone. You can't see an invisible man, but you can hear him breathing, and he leaves wet feet on wet stone.

Yamoch ran into the water. Luth went in after him. Yamoch put two lightning bolts through him, one after the other, and Luth kept going and caught him in the water anyway.

It was Luth who came back up out of that water, alone. He said nothing about it, and I didn't ask, and that is the most respectful thing I have ever done.

Which left the rest of us between a hydra in the opening to the river and the yuan-ti coming down the passage from the main hall.

So: the hydra-grenade polymorph.

I turned the hydra into a turtle, and Ofar picked the turtle up.

Ofar threw the turtle down the passage to the main hall, straight onto the head of the first yuan-ti in it, and the yuan-ti died. The turtle had taken so much of that blow itself that the spell broke, and it turned back into a hydra, there in the passage, which had been cut for snakes and was a great deal too narrow for anything that size.

It stuck.

Five heads faced the yuan-ti, with no room to turn round; they couldn't get past it, it couldn't get back to us, and the way to the river was free. I have never loved an animal so much.

I'd like to say we planned it from the start, but I am a very bad liar, and we didn't.

ONE THROW. PERFECT. I SHALL TELL IT AT EVERY FIRE TILL I DIE. OLLI'S SPELL HELPED. A LITTLE.

Luth missed all of it, being in the water with Yamoch; Ofar has told him since.

Then we ran. Along the river under the Fane, Ofar and I on Jambo, his lizard, along the cave wall above the water, sideways on the rock, faster than anything with legs should go on a wall at all.

Then something shot him; I never saw what. Jambo went to light in the middle of a stride, the way summoned things go, and there was nothing under us but air, and then water.

We fell in. I came up spluttering and paddled for the dark line of the bank, while Ofar, in all his armour, went down like a dropped anchor.

ARMOUR SINKS, AND SO DID I. FOR A TIME THE WATER WAS STRONGER THAN MY COURAGE.

Vaeril had the magic rope, and at a word it had bound itself fast to Ofar, down there in the dark. Vaeril was pulling with everything he had. Ofar, by then, had begun to panic.

Ofar panicked underwater and got up to exhaustion 4, nearly dying.

That's where it stopped for us that night, too: Ofar under the water, and Vaeril pulling. I'll stop here as well. Fair is fair.

9 to 10 Mirtul · under the palace

In my notes from that night it says Vaeril pulled Ofar ashore "like a water-skier", and Ofar has asked me to cross that out. It was under the water the whole way, along the bottom, on the rope, until the rock came up out of the dark and Ofar got one hand on it.

He came out so empty he couldn't lift his head, and he very nearly didn't come out at all. The last yuan-ti on that shore didn't last long.

I swam ashore and heaved Yamoch's body up after me; it had no head any more, and I didn't ask about that either.

I CAME OUT MORE DEAD THAN ALIVE, DRAGGED UNDER WATER THE WHOLE WAY. VAERIL NEVER LET GO OF THE ROPE. I AM IN HIS DEBT.

Then Vaeril found a room of prisoners with a single yuan-ti guarding them.

Vaeril killed him, and I promptly un-killed him.

My zombie led Vaeril towards the dungeon. When the dumb python got in the way, the zombie stayed behind to fight it, so Vaeril could run on.

It didn't come back. It was a good zombie, and I want that written down somewhere.

Vaeril and I split up. He went in, deeper, to free more prisoners and to look for my brother, because that is what we all believed then: that Tarkil was a prisoner somewhere down there.

I went out with the freed people. We sent three ahead to draw attention away, and one of them ran into Luth's ravens; we passed him on the way, and I am not going to describe it.

A little boy walked beside me the whole way, and I told him how Ofar the hero killed Ras Nsi.

What Vaeril did in there, he told us later.

He had seen an owlin about to be sacrificed, flown in invisible, grabbed him, and dimension-doored five hundred feet straight up, which nearly drove him mad. They came down on a roof, and he forced a healing potion down the other owlin's beak.

Ofar wrote it down like this:

VAERIL BRINGS TARKIL OUT. STRAIGHT UP.

And that is what we all thought: Vaeril had saved my brother.

Remember that. I'll come back to it.

I'm keeping my promise to tell it in order, and it is very hard.

Outside, the Red Wizards were waiting at the tunnel mouth. They're our enemies now: that happens when your Red Wizard escort turns into an invisible son of a bitch. They shot at Luth until he nearly died.

We pulled back into the passage, Luth and Ofar and me and four of the freed people, and I put up my Tiny Hut: a dome of force, ten feet every way. It sealed off both cave mouths at once. Nothing was getting in.

Then Ofar chewed his drumbassar, the leaf from home, and then he found the wall.

AFTER THE DRUMBASSAR, I RECALL THE WALL. THE WALL LOST.

Behind the wall: a thin crack in the rock, where you could hear the river. Luth oiled himself all over and climbed in.

And got stuck.

He got through in the end, into a cellar under the house next door.

By then the yuan-ti were coming from one side and the Red Wizards from the other, and the Red Wizards made my hut disappear.

We had two bombs, from the thieves' guild boss back in Port Nyanzaru. And I had an idea.

10 Mirtul · after midnight · the tunnels

The Red Wizards came into the caves. I held their woman fast with everything I had, and she cast a fireball anyway.

Not all of the people we'd freed got up again.

One of the fighters took her head off.

Then Ofar became a bomb martyr.

Ofar had two small bombs and wanted to collapse the cave with them, but they were quite weak. He rolled two natural 20s with them, though, which I ruled was good enough to bring down that whole section of the cave. And it had to come down. The Red Wizards were strong and well rested, and the party had just come out of a boss fight: Ofar had nearly drowned and was at exhaustion 4, Luth'ayen had no spell slots left, Oliver was only halfway through becoming a wizard, and the real Tarkil and Vaeril had teleported away, so the party was split. Only the three of them and a few NPCs were in that cave. Without the bombs this could very well have been a total party kill.

Two bombs, two perfect throws, and the roof came down between us and them, which also meant that there was no way out.

So I raised two of the dead, and the headless woman I polymorphed into a giant badger: undead, and still without a head.

It nearly flattened the boy the moment it moved, and Ofar had to put him back together; then the badger dug, and we followed it.

A CHILD IN THE WAY. I HEAL HIM ERE HE CAN CRY. WE MOVE ON.

In the tunnels lay two dead yuan-ti, rimed with frost. Somebody with ice had been here before us.

And in a cellar vault: Artus Cimber and Dragonbait. Artus, the man Xandala told us was her father, months ago on the ship. Dragonbait is a saurial, a lizard-man with a holy sword (a legendary one, a holy avenger), and a lot calmer than his name.

They were waiting behind the pillars with longbows drawn, ready for a fight. They didn't trust us. In the end they gave us a healing potion.

Artus had a Red Wizard down there with him, a mercenary, half frozen and nearly dead, and was asking him questions. When we left the room, the questions stopped.

They'll fight the Red Wizards with us, but they won't come into the tomb.

THE FROZEN WIZARD HAD TOLD ALL HE KNEW. AS WE LEFT, ARTUS ENDED HIM. A HARD MAN; DOWN HERE, ONLY HARD MEN LIVE.

10 Mirtul · noon · fog and drizzle

The badger dug us up and up, under the river (we think), and at last out.

Daylight.

We came up outside the palace walls into fog and drizzle at noon, and twenty minutes later the badger was just a dead woman again.

Then across the river on Luth's Water Walk. We left my zombies behind, since they'd be too loud in the water, and then Ofar was loud in the water instead; good thing we left the zombies.

Back at the old safehouse, the people we had freed told us the yuan-ti took them a few weeks ago. Now they have names in my book:

Korin. Hochi. Semra. And the boy, Merli.

THE SNAKES TOOK THEM WEEKS AGO. HOW MANY DID THEY TAKE BEFORE, FOR WHOM NO ONE CAME?

After the rest we went out again, with Jambo. Outside, two owlins were waiting for us.

One was Vaeril.

Remember when Vaeril saved my brother? Five hundred feet straight up?

Vaeril is Tarkil.

The Tarkil, the one "Vaeril" told me was my brother. Three days ago he knocked on a shrine door in a green hood and told us he was somebody else, and the owlin he carried off that altar is the real Vaeril.

Is he my brother? He thinks so, but he isn't sure either, and nobody else is.

I came to Chult for the souls of my family in Baldur's Gate. I did not expect to find, maybe, the other half of my family wearing a green hood and lying to me.

IN THE SAFEHOUSE HE HID THINGS IN HIS CLOAK. I WROTE IT DOWN. NOW I KNOW WHAT HE HID. A NAME.

And then he lectured me about how I am not trustworthy, he who had been lying to us the whole time.

He has my feathers, exactly my feathers; I checked.

We fetched the real Vaeril and went round to Artus, who was at a tower nearby with Dragonbait. There we shot an invisible imp out of the sky; I think it's the one that has been following us since the shrines.

OLLI TELLS THEM AT ONCE THAT HE IS A NECROMANCER. OF COURSE HE DOES.

So now we are allies, and the plan is the palace, and the Red Wizards.

At the south-west wall there was a hidden rope. Luth climbed up and looked over, and on the other side there was light, and screaming.

Tarkil heard it too. He says it was Nimriel, the third of their scouts, his friend. His ears have been ringing ever since.

An alliance of necessity. Artus keeps his ringed hand close whenever Oliver speaks of the dead, and Dragonbait watches me the way a paladin watches the priest of another god. We share an enemy and nothing else. It will hold until the Red Wizards fall, and perhaps not one breath longer. — L.

10 Mirtul · night · over the wall

Luth went over first and came down the other side with a crash; then Jambo broke a stone off the wall, loudly, and came back for Ofar.

Orvex stayed at the safehouse with Korin, Hochi, Semra and Merli.

Getting seven of us and a lizard over a wall in the dark took a while: two owlins by wing, and one very much not. In the end everyone was over.

TWO OWLINS AND OLLI WHISPER IN A CORNER. I GUARD THE LIZARD. SOMEONE MUST.

The plan: the building where they were doing the ritual. Artus, Dragonbait, Vaeril and I through the front door. Ofar, Luth and Tarkil on Jambo, up the wall and in through the windows in the roof.

I summoned some undead of my own, just to have company.

The roof team, all three of them and the lizard, managed the loudest sneaking in the history of sneaking.

ON A LIZARD WE CRASH THROUGH A ROOF WINDOW. STEALTH WAS NEVER THE PLAN.

Inside sat Zagmira at a golden harp, with her Red Wizards around her, and the dead.

Every time she played, the dead got up and danced. Around the harp there was something like a bubble: spells slid off it, and fighting inside it was like fighting in syrup.

We fought on two fronts, and it was close.

There was one dead owlin among the dancers.

Tarkil saw her before I understood: Nimriel, the screams from the wall.

Nimriel went down as a zombie, for good this time, and when she fell Tarkil dropped where he stood, until Vaeril brought him round.

Afterwards Luth prayed over all of us, and it worked.

CALL PU'ULUA FOR NIMRIEL? TARKIL KNOWS A TALE OF HER. I KNOW ONE ALSO. IT IS ABOUT TEA.

In the middle of it all, Xandala came through the door. Xandala, the half-elf with the dragon scales we pulled out of the sea on the way to Chult, who said she was looking for her father. She raised her hand at Artus, and I counterspelled her.

She left, and we caught our breath.

Then she came back, and this time she got him. Artus's eyes went empty, he turned, and he cast a sphere of ice into the room.

ICE. I GO DOWN. I RISE. OUTSIDE SHE FIGHTS ARTUS AND DRAGONBAIT. NOT OUR FIGHT. WE HAVE OUR OWN.

I don't think she was ever really looking for her father.

Then we looted the rest of the house. Ofar says I'm not allowed to list it.

Zagmira's staff was lying outside, and of course I took it.

And the cubes, all the rest of them: we have every one now.

And then I found

PAPER!!!!!!!

The tunnel in Artus's cellar was still full of water, so we dug a new one, near the safehouse, and I put up my hut, and everyone slept and meditated. Everyone except me. I had three days to write down.

OLLI HAS FOUND PAPER. NOW HE WRITES INSTEAD OF TALKING. PEACE, AT LAST.

In the night, Valindra sent Luth a message: the Red Wizards were weak, she has more about the Soulmonger, come and see her in her tower. Valindra, the elf from the Heart of Ubtao, who sent us to Omu in the first place.

So here we are, all caught up; from now on I write it as it happens.

11 Mirtul, or 12 · morning

I've lost count of the days. Down here they all look the same, and they all smell of yuan-ti.

A reminder, for whoever finds this book without the first one: we are in Omu because somewhere under this city sits the Soulmonger, the thing that holds on to the souls of the dead. It is why Ofar's curse gets worse every week, why Syndra is dying, and why my family, killed at the wedding, is still waiting under a spell. Break it, and they can come back. That is the whole plan.

This morning we split up. Ofar and Tarkil went invisible into the palace, to fetch the glaive of the old king, Na'Nbuzo. Luth and I walked the rescued Chultans out of the city.

TARKIL AND I, UNSEEN, STRAIGHT TO THE GLAIVE. NO DETOURS.

Before that, Tarkil climbed onto a broken wall and asked his patron, one of the Wind Dukes, six questions out loud, so we heard the answers when he did:

  • Can we bring Nimriel back, if we break the curse down there? Yes.
  • Are we strong enough to break it? Unclear.
  • Is a piece of the Rod of Law in the tomb? Yes.
  • And the skull chalice of Ch'gakare? The tomb.
  • Is Olli my brother?

Yes.

He found out in the same moment I did. All that "maybe", and then one word out of the wind.

I WROTE IT IN THE TUNNELS ALREADY. NOW THE WIND SAYS IT TOO. GOOD. ONE QUESTION FEWER.

I wasn't there for the glaive. Ofar was, with Tarkil. So Ofar wrote this part himself, in his own hand. I haven't changed a word.

THE GLAIVE OF THE KING LAY UPON AN ALTAR OF STONE, HELD FAST BY TWO RODS OF IRON. NO LOCK. NO RIDDLE. WHO WOULD BEAR IT MUST TEAR IT FREE.

FIRST THE KING CAME, NA'NBUZO HIMSELF, OUT OF THE GREY HALLS OF THE DEAD. WE SPOKE LONG. WHAT HE SAID IS MINE TO KEEP. THEN HE STOOD BEHIND ME AND WATCHED.

I SET BOTH HANDS UPON THE SHAFT. IT BURNED. NOT AS FIRE BURNS THE SKIN: IT BURNED WITHIN, AND WHERE MY STRENGTH WENT OUT, LIGHT CAME IN. I DID NOT LET GO.

THE RODS BENT. THE ALTAR CRACKED, THEN BURST ASUNDER, AND THE GLAIVE WAS IN MY HANDS.

I HAVE KNOWN PAIN. THIS WAS MORE. I WOULD BEAR IT AGAIN.

I was on the far side of Omu when it happened, walking the rescued Chultans out of the city, and I heard him scream. The whole city must have heard it. So that is Ofar's version, and Ofar tells things big; this time, I think, he told it the right size.

A long shaft of dark bronze and gold, red ribbons at the collar, and a curved golden blade with an edge that glows like a coal you've just blown on. It was made for a king. It is supposed to make whoever carries it look like one. On Ofar, that wasn't much work.

Then we went to see Valindra in her tower. "The Red Wizards are dead? Ah, lovely," she said. I don't think she meant it as a condolence.

The Soulmonger, she says, gathers souls to make a god, and if we destroy it, everyone dies. So we should bring it to her, and she will let the souls go, gently.

BRING IT TO HER? NAY. WE BREAK IT. I BEAR NO GOD-MAKER TO A SMILING ELF.

While she talked, I raised a few of the dead; it seemed polite, with so many of them lying about. She didn't comment, and that worried me more than if she had.

The tomb, she said, belongs to Acererak, a lich. I have written that word in this book before, and it never gets any better.

afternoon · the Tomb of the Nine Gods

At the foot of the northern cliffs stands an obelisk: Acererak's welcome, a warning and six rules, all of them riddles. Only one of them stuck.

Speak no truth to the doomed child.

Finally a rule written for me, and I will fail it, obviously, because I fail every rule that asks me to lie.

Eight statues of the trickster gods stand there, and a ninth is missing: Unkh, who could never make up her mind.

UNKH CANNOT DECIDE. A GOD WHO CANNOT DECIDE IS OF USE TO NO ONE.

A door had eight sockets for our cubes, so we tried a half-random combination.

A stone block came down behind us, green gas poured from the skulls' mouths, and one Dimension Door scroll later we were outside again, coughing.

The real way in was hidden, and behind it lay a pit.

Across the pit, a devil's face in the wall, its open mouth filled with a darkness deeper than any shadow. Something used to live in there.

Then a shaft going down, balconies all the way round and no bottom that I can see, and on every level a brass plaque with more riddles.

Everybody here writes in riddles. I'm starting to miss Port Nyanzaru, where people just lie to your face.

the same evening · level one

The tomb has nine gods in it, one for each trickster, and each one has a room that wants something from you. First, Obo'laka: six dead in black masks on thrones, and a bronze disc covered in eyes. The eyes move. We came out with a ring, and all of us came out.

My zombie Toriff drank from a fountain of marble maidens, and then he burst.

I wrote "experiment: inconclusive". Ofar says that's not what the word means. Toriff, at least, has concluded.

Somewhere in here, a letter from Devlin Bashir, the last of the Company of the Yellow Banner. They got this far. "His final secret always leads to your doom. Tymora save us all." Underneath, in another hand, someone had added a line about the Eye of Zaltec: that it can bring back the dead. I copied it out and underlined it twice.

Level two: Papazotl, the bird god. Bow as the dead god intoned, so we bowed, to nobody, and the hunter on a bronze shield peeled out of the metal and threw his spear at me.

He missed.

I BOWED. TO NO ONE. IT WORKED.

still the same night, I think · levels two and three

The hunter kept throwing at me, only me, until a Magic Missile of mine cut through the straps his shield hung on and it fell off the wall like a plate. My zombie Schmorif put on the amulet from the coffin and grew big and strong.

On the next level, three curtains, and behind the last one a boar's head, chewing.

Tarkil walked towards it without a word, as if something were drawing him in on a line, and he would have put his head between its tusks if we hadn't caught hold of him and pulled him back.

Afterwards he said nothing about it. Brothers, apparently, also have that in common.

In Kubazan's tomb, the froghemoth's god, Ofar got the riddle wrong.

A RIDDLE ANSWERED WRONGLY, AND THE GHOSTS DRANK DEEP OF MY LIFE. I WOULD HAVE IT BACK.

In the coffin: bracers. I touched them, and Kubazan went into me. Suddenly I was terribly strong, and I stopped being careful. I liked it, which is the frightening part. In the end the bracers, and the god, went to Vaeril.

The ring from the mask room went to Luth, and Obo'laka with it.

Then, by accident, I touched Papazotl's amulet, and Papazotl went into me and told me to kill myself.

I stabbed myself once before they got hold of me. In the end I got myself back. Under all the gods there is still a me, and he is stubborn.

The amulet is with Tarkil now, under his shirt, where nobody touches it.

For the record: I have now been a frog god, a bird god, and an owlin, all on one evening.

Moa's tomb admits only one of us, so of course it was me.

Inside, in a crystal box on a pedestal, floats a tiny skull, a child's, and a little girl's voice asked me who I was.

I told her that her papa was waiting outside, that we were here to rescue her, and that there was a surprise for her: cake.

The kindest lie of my life, and the only good one.

ONLY ONE MAY ENTER: HE WHO CANNOT LIE. HE LIED. I AM PROUD OF HIM.

In her coffin lay a staff with a python on it. I touched it. Green smoke wound itself around me, and now Moa lives in me too.

Since then I have to tell the truth. Always.

I would like to point out that nothing about my life has changed.

We made her a promise, the girl: when the Soulmonger is gone, we come back and break her skull, so she can go. I wrote it here so we can't forget.

Then a green, steaming font, in a room where every shadow comes loose from its owner and does the opposite of what he does. The font wanted a shadow to drink from it. The way to manage that, it turns out, is to hold Tarkil upside down in front of it.

That makes six crystal eyes, and next door is I'jin.

later · level three · I'jin

I'jin's door is covered in hundreds of carved locusts, and you open it by pressing exactly one of them. Guess which.

Inside, a dead dwarf of the Yellow Banner, still holding two crystal eyes. He kept them to the end.

HE HELD THE EYES TO THE END. WE CARRY THEM ON. THUS ARE THE DEAD THANKED.

The floor was another riddle; I read, the others hopped. I'jin's horn went to Vaeril, and I'jin with it: suddenly he moves like a cat that has had coffee.

Then a room that is mostly hole, with wooden discs drifting over it. Tarkil flew across, of course, and I watched him go and thought about my wings.

Gods living in the party so far: Kubazan (in Vaeril, with the bracers), Papazotl (in Tarkil, with the amulet under his shirt), Obo'laka (in Luth), Moa (in me), I'jin (in Vaeril again; he collects them).

Down, past a stone golem, and then we had all ten eyes.

A STONE GOLEM. MY GLAIVE ON STONE: SPARKS. IT LOST.

We sat down with our backs against a big round mirror set into a door, with ten empty holes around it, and rested, and in the mirror my reflection wrote along with me, always slightly faster.

after the rest · the mirror door

The ten eyes went into the ten holes around the mirror, one by one, and with every eye the owl in the mirror got older. One eye: a grey feather. Four: his ear tufts drooped. Seven: his beak had gone yellow and his back bent. At ten, an ancient owlin looked back at me, half bald, eyes milky, still holding this book. I put my pen down. So did he, a moment later.

The door opened onto a round vault, its floor polished like a mirror, candles everywhere, and in the middle of the air a black silk cloth draped over something round.

We saw nothing else at all.

Then rays started coming out of the empty air.

A BEHOLDER NONE CAN SEE. YET IT CAN BE STRUCK. I STRIKE WHENCE THE RAYS COME.

One of the rays caught Luth, and Luth turned to stone, from the boots up.

We won anyway, and then we looked at Luth.

He looked very surprised, for a statue, his shield up and his mouth open as if he had been about to say something important; knowing Luth, he had.

The plan, and I promise this is what actually happened:

  • Vaeril and Tarkil fly all the way up the shaft to the fountain on the first level, the one that killed Toriff, and fill a waterskin. (They tried, at least. They managed.)
  • Someone turns stone-Luth into an anglerfish, because a fish can drink.
  • We pour the water into the fish.

The fountain is a gamble. It came up the good way, and Luth's stone went away.

Then the fish's own guardian spirit hit Tarkil, because it decided Tarkil was an enemy. Tarkil is still offended. Then Luth was Luth again, damp and polite, and everything was fine.

LUTH AS A FISH: UGLY, BUT ALIVE. THAT WAS THE AIM.

We slept in the vault. Well, we slept, Luth meditated, and a hundred candles burned all night without getting any shorter.

When we got up we were all stronger, and Ofar had back the life the ghosts drank from him, or nearly all of it.

THE GHOSTS KEEP ONE. LET THEM. I KNOW WHERE THEY DWELL.

morning · level four

Ofar and Tarkil woke up bleeding from the eyes. It was the curse, of course; we all knew it, and nobody said it. We wiped it off and went on, because that is what we do now.

At the bottom of the great shaft, gargoyles guarded a skeleton whose skull is the key: out of its crown grows a great block of grey carved bone, as big as the skull itself, with a triangle cut into it. There are five of these walking keys in the tomb, each crowned with a different shape. We have the first.

And in a devil's mouth in the wall, Luth found Billy: a small, very calm lizard, and apparently a clever one. He is coming with us; nobody voted, and nobody needed to.

BLOOD IN MINE EYES. STILL I SEE THE KEY.

A skeleton in the wall held a burning candle. We blew it out, and the room took us into the dark: no light, no magic, no air. Tarkil broke the right bones, and we could breathe again.

Then Shagambi's tomb: forty-eight clay warriors, kneeling in silence. I counted them twice. Nobody moved, and that was the best thing that happened all day.

Then a small room, sand trickling from the ceiling, and a medusa carved in the wall holding a lit red candle.

Someone pressed the onyx on her necklace, and all four of us were in a small cell, and the sand came faster.

Luth has his shield up in front of her face, Tarkil has his hand on the onyx, and the sand is at my shins. I'm writing this because writing it down is what I do when I'm frightened.

It's rising.

Level four · the sand cell

Where I stopped last time: four of us in a little room filling up with sand, and Ofar outside the cells, waiting for us.

Then the floor split, and underneath it stone rollers with teeth turned towards each other. I looked at them for exactly as long as it takes to understand a thing like that.

Then Tarkil got us out. One moment there were teeth turning under our feet, and the next we were standing in the corridor beside Ofar, who had never looked so surprised or so glad.

I WAITED OUTSIDE THE CELLS. MINUTES PASSED AND NONE CAME OUT. MY FOOT WAS ON THE THRESHOLD TO GO IN AFTER THEM WHEN FOUR FOOLS APPEARED OUT OF NOTHING BESIDE ME. THE BEST HOUR OF THE DAY.
These rollers would have dealt 24d10 force damage, 132 on average, and the whole cell sits in an antimagic field. That would have killed every one of them easily. Who designs such traps?

We were in Shagambi's tomb, where a mandolin lay on the sarcophagus; every god down here jumps into whoever touches its relic.

Luth touched it first, and the mandolin didn't want him.

Then Ofar touched it, and Shagambi went into him. He stood very still for a moment and then said it felt good. That is not what the rest of us said about our gods.

SHAGAMBI DWELLS IN ME NOW. THE MANDOLIN I PLAY NOT. I STRIKE FASTER.

Orvex, our scribe, says the door we want is on level six, all the way down.

Level five · the gears

Down the rope Ofar insists is called the Schlingelidingdong, and then: the mixing desk. It runs the whole level: the rooms on this floor are giant cogs, and this thing turns them.

I have never been happier in a tomb.

The red dial puts a voice in your head. The others teased it. I couldn't: every time it asked me something, I answered. Honestly. It is asking me right now what I'm writing. I told it.

We turned the rooms. On the way Luth and I fell into the lake. Briefly. Luth would like that word underlined. Briefly.

A door grew a wet mouth and wanted something alive. It very nearly had Ofar, before we fed it a glowing crab from the lake instead.

Then Ofar fell in the water as well, and laughed, for a whole minute; he couldn't stop and he couldn't say why, and when it was over he stood up and was completely serious again, and nobody said anything.

I like him very much.

THAT WAS THE WATER, NOT I. NOR WAS THAT TO BE WRITTEN DOWN.

The golden mastodon

A life-sized golden mastodon on a great stone cog. We fitted the bone keys and plugged in the lever, and everything turned: fire from the floor in rings, four devils out of the fire, and the stone block over the door came down and stopped a hand's width above the floor.

Twenty centimetres.

We were on the wrong side of the block, and so were the devils.

Level five · under the door

The devils kept coming, nastier each time. Tarkil and I fought side by side, brothers. I threw a Thunder Orb into the middle of them.

It broke over them like a wave over rocks, and when the noise had rolled away down the corridor, there were a great many fewer devils.

Ofar and Luth fought them through the gap under the block, lying flat on their bellies and poking; it looked ridiculous, and it worked.

THE BLOCK DID NOT CLOSE. BENEATH IT WE HAD STACKED THE SKELETON KEYS, AND THOSE DO NOT BREAK. THUS THE 20 CM, AND THROUGH THEM I THRUST, EVERY TIME.

When the last devil stopped trying, smoke gathered into something holding up a cup: the Skull Chalice of Ch'gakare, the thing Princess Mwaxanaré sent us for. It looked exactly like my drawing. I'm prouder of that than I should be.

Tarkil put it away very quickly, the way you put a thing away that you were sent for.

TARKIL TAKES THE CUP. NONE ASKS. I SHALL ASK, LATER.

Then Tarkil cast Seeming on all of us: Ofar and Luth are huge stone golems now, Tarkil and I two scruffy dwarves (I can see my own beak if I squint), and my zombie Schmorif looks exactly like Orvex, so we call him Schmorvex.

And Billy was made as conspicuous as possible.

A hat with stars, a beard, a monocle, a red cape and a staff with a glowing orb: he looks fantastic, and he knows it. It is my favourite thing in the whole tomb.

Disguised like that, we went through five wardrobes into five worlds and fought whatever came out of each. In the fog of a graveyard the door swung shut behind Schmorvex, who had never once complained about anything, and I didn't get to say goodbye.

I AM A GOLEM NOW. I SEEM SLOW. GOOD. LET THEM THINK LITTLE OF ME.

Level five · the last wardrobe

The last wardrobe let out a bone devil, all spine and hooks. We killed it, and the main gate opened onto a corridor of fog, and at the end, an iron bull's head in an archway.

Luth was already stepping into it when, on some instinct, I tossed a coin in ahead of him and watched it come apart in the air. Whatever the fog was, it would have eaten everything he carried. So I sent Gorkus, my newest zombie, and the fog took his clothes off him in threads and then in nothing. He didn't mind; he pulled the iron ring out of the bull's nose, and the bull fell apart.

I took notes: wool goes first, then linen, then leather. Hair doesn't go at all; it just stands up. It is useful to know these things.

Level six · the Sisters' hall

Down on the last level: a hall full of green fog, rocking chairs, workbenches heaped with buttons and thread, and a rusty iron cage.

The fog came out of a bronze cauldron in the middle. Breathing it made you want to sit down in one of the rocking chairs and stay. We knocked it over.

Then three dolls came out of the smoke: a straw doll full of rusty pins, a clay child with no face, and a stuffed monkey that was a unicycle from the waist down.

They wanted to be rescued.

In the cage sat Luth.

Our own Luth was standing next to me; this one had the same white hair and the same face, and his eyes were a little too wet.

Back in the jungle a demon monkey bothered us every night. Later Orvex told us what it had been stealing: Luth's hair.

Luth opened the cage, healed him, and talked to him for a while. I didn't hear what they said, and for once in my life I didn't ask.

TWO LUTHS. ONE IS ENOUGH. THAT I DID NOT SAY ALOUD.

Then Luth cast Hallow.

A circle of white light spread across the floor. The fog drew back from its edge like a dog from fire. And inside it, all at once, there were three women.

The Sewn Sisters.

They had been there the whole time. Widow Groat, with gold coins over her eyes and red ants in her sleeves: her ants have been eating Ofar's nights since the first one we spent together. Peggy Deadbells, green and swollen. Baggy Nanna, whose face is a sewn-up sack.

Inside the circle, Moa went quiet, and for the first time in days I could have lied. I didn't; I only wanted to know that I could.

And then we fought them, all of us at once, Tarkil's sword, Luth's hammer, Ofar's glaive and my dead, and for once nobody tripped over anybody.

FOR ONCE, ALL GOES WELL. I TRUST IT NOT.
WIDOW GROAT. I HAVE SEEN HER FACE. NO COINS SHALL HIDE IT FROM ME NOW.

We gave them a proper beating, and then, right in the middle of it, they took hold of their amulets and blinked away.

The other Luth lay on the floor between living and dying, with ours standing over him.

THEY WILL RETURN. TO ME THEY ALWAYS RETURN. I SHALL BE READY.

Level six · the Sisters' rooms

Luth finished his double with his boot. Nobody said anything, and nobody will.

We packed up the dolls, and Ofar carries them, or they ride on him; it's hard to say which.

Orvex reads to them. Every time we stop, he sits the three of them in a row and reads them a story out of one of the hags' books, in his careful scribe's voice, every comma read out loud.

Then Widow Groat's room: a bed of blackened gold coins with a body's shape pressed into it, red ants everywhere, and a shelf of jars with eyes in them. When we came in, they all turned to look at us.

Ofar broke every jar.

THE EYES FIRST. WHEN SHE RETURNS, SHE SHALL BE BLIND.

In the third room, leather sacks hung on chains from the ceiling, and some of them twitched: they were stomachs.

From one of them came a muffled cawing.

Inside was a raven, half digested down to the bone and still moving. Luth said the raven was a guide, sent for him, and I made him give it a name; or rather, I gave it one, and he let me.

Peter.

Peter showed Luth the way to the door one last time. Then Luth gave him an honourable death, the Raven Queen's way, with the toll of a single bell. Peter had been dead a long time already, and the Raven Queen suffers nothing to walk that should be at rest.

HE SLEW HIS OWN RAVEN, GENTLY. I KNEW NOT THAT IT COULD BE DONE.

On the back wall hung a big cracked mirror, and above it, in dried blood: PIGGY PIGGY PIGGY. To see anything in it, you have to say it. So I said it.

The Sisters, round a pillar of light full of souls, and one of them feeding them to an enormous, ugly baby. That is where the souls go: all the dead of Chult who can't come back, Ofar's village, my family. Luth had to carry me out of the room. I couldn't stop looking.

OLLI SEES WHERE THE SOULS GO. I SEE WHERE TO STRIKE.

The last room was a kitchen, where a thin butler in a dusty black suit offered us little glazed cakes.

They were cursed, so we declined, rudely, and Ofar threw the butler out; by the time we were done with him he was a scarecrow.

Orvex says the dolls are children's souls. The Sisters tried things out on them first. Luth's double was one of their tests.

Tarkil said we shouldn't speak badly of the Sisters, and nobody knows why; I don't think he does either.

Then the others wanted to open the gate, quietly, so that I wouldn't notice.

I noticed. Something in me wanted nobody ever to open it, and something in Ofar wanted to open it himself. Our gods had an argument, and we had it for them: Gorkus and Jambo went for each other, and I tried to put a fireball on Ofar while he was invisible, and then I actually did.

I'm sorry, Ofar. It's in writing now.

And then the Sisters came back.

We killed them. All three.

WIDOW GROAT IS DEAD. MY OATH IS KEPT. WHO STRUCK LAST MATTERS NOT. (OLLI'S FIREBALL: FORGIVEN. ALMOST.)

Luth talked Ofar into one more long rest before the gate.

That night the pain came for Ofar one more time: the ants, the blood, all of it, and worse than ever.

In the morning he wrote two words in his book and showed them to nobody, but I saw them anyway: LAST TIME.

We put the four keys into the gate, and it opened.

Level six · the nursery

Behind the gate, black marble stairs went down into a hall shaped like a triangle, with crumbling balconies all round it and, far below them, a pool of lava.

Over the lava, on three metal struts as wide as bridges, hung a crystal cylinder as tall as a house, full of pale shapes going round and round and screaming. Four long tentacles grew out of its lid.

And next to it, floating, tied to it by a twisted cord: the baby from the mirror. As big as an elephant, shrivelled and wet, its arms and legs gone thin, its head far too big and dripping black.

Orvex calls it an atropal, a god that hasn't been born yet, and the cylinder is the Soulmonger. Every soul it has taken from Chult, every soul that couldn't come back, has been going down that cord.

So this is what has been eating the dead.

ONE CYLINDER. ONE MONSTROUS CHILD. THREE STRUTS. THOSE ARE THE TARGETS. WE GO DOWN READY.

Our gods woke up. Moa, in me, wanted the souls set free; Obo'laka, in Luth, was afraid the bones in the alcoves would get up; Shagambi, in Ofar, wanted the thing destroyed, and at once.

We had prepared everything before we turned the keys, spells ready, weapons out, Billy in a bag, and standing at the top of those stairs it didn't feel like nearly enough.

I'm writing this afterwards, on a broken balcony above the cooling lava, with soot on the page. For once I remember the order. I don't think I'll ever forget it.

First, the Soulmonger.

Moa wanted the souls free, and for once every god in every one of us agreed with mine. We went for the cylinder. I won't pretend I know whose blow cracked it; all of us claim it, and all of us are a little bit right.

It burst, and the pieces came down around us like a crystal rain, and the souls went free.

Thousands upon thousands of little lights, so many that the whole vault filled with them and I couldn't see Ofar two steps away. Then round and up, faster and faster, and gone in a flash so white I could still see it the next day.

I looked for my family in the light. Owen, Ophelia, Orville. When the priests tried to bring them back, it didn't work, as if something were holding them. This was the something. I don't know if souls have faces. I looked anyway.

Then the atropal.

Without its food it was only a very large, very angry baby that had never been born, and it screamed, and died.

THE UNHOLY THING IS DEAD. SHAGAMBI FALLS SILENT. I DO NOT.

And then he came.

No sound. Only a cold that crept into my bones, and the light flickering and ducking like an animal in front of its master. Then he was standing on the south balcony: a skeleton older than kingdoms, in robes that smelled of a thousand years, a staff with a skull on top, two white sparks where his eyes should be.

Next to him floated a ball of nothing, a hole where the world simply stopped, and everything in me screamed not to look at it.

Acererak.

That's what he said. And that he would make himself a new one, and our souls would be its foundation stone.

His eyes slid over what was left of the atropal the way you look at a cup you've broken. Then they slid over us.

Acererak's first action was Time Stop, a 9th-level spell, the highest there is. It gives him 1d4+1 turns in a row. I had written a long monologue for him, and a plan for what he would do if he rolled a 4. He rolled a 1, which got him just one extra action for a 9th-level spell. Fortunately for the players.

He said: "Time is my servant, and I bid it be silent."

I blinked. In that blink Luth's Hallow was gone from the floor, as if somebody had wiped it away, and Tarkil was lying on the stone.

Somewhere inside that blink he had spoken. I don't know how I know the words. They were simply in my head afterwards, the way a bad dream is:

"No god has power in this place. Only I."

And to Tarkil: "No god watches over you, no trickster laughs at your side. Alone you came, alone you shall go." Then a long silence. Then one word.

"Die."

He had stopped time, though he hadn't got much of it, and he spent it on two things: he broke our Hallow, and he killed my brother.

My brother. I had only just found out he was one.

THE BONE KING STOPS TIME. I SEE IT NOT. I SEE ONLY TARKIL FALL. I HATE MAGIC I CANNOT STRIKE.

He wasn't finished. He looked down at the dead atropal and said: "Rise, my child. Even in death you shall serve me."

And it rose, bigger than before, grey and wrong, its cords hanging off it like wet rope: dead, and moving anyway.

I did the only thing I could think of: I grabbed Ofar by the arm and Dimension Doored the two of us onto Acererak's balcony, right next to him. Ofar says it was my best idea ever. Ofar says that about every idea that ends with him standing next to something he can hit.

Acererak pointed one finger at Ofar, and a thin green ray came out of it. I tried to counter it, and it didn't work.

So I did the other thing, and pulled it onto me.

I don't know how to describe a Disintegrate from the inside. Every feather I own tried to leave in a different direction, and then it stopped, and I was still there, mostly, and very surprised about it.

Acererak decided he didn't like his balcony any more and rose into the air, to float away over the lava, out of reach.

Ofar had been saving something: the one bit of luck you keep back for a single moment in your life. He spent it.

One perfect blow.

The blow nailed Acererak to the air so that he couldn't move a foot, and then Ofar hit him, and hit him, and hit him, the king's glaive burning like a coal. I have never seen anything take damage like that, and I don't think Acererak had either.

It didn't kill him. He threw the green ray at us again, and we lived through that too. Then he hung over the lava, out of reach, and for what felt like an age that is how it stayed: green rays from him, a poison cloud from the dead atropal, and the ball of nothing drifting across the balcony while we tried not to be wherever it was going.

THE LUCK I KEPT FOR ONE HOUR, I SPENT. THE BONE KING STAYS WHERE HE IS. THEN I STRIKE HIM, AGAIN AND AGAIN.

And in all of that, Luth.

He was out on the wreck of the Soulmonger, which had come down nearly flat across its struts, on his knees next to Tarkil, a diamond going to dust in his fist and his other hand on Tarkil's chest. It could work now, because the Soulmonger was broken: the dead could come back again. Tarkil coughed.

Then Luth stood up and called down an angel, a huge one, all wings and light, and it went straight for Acererak.

DEATH CAME FOR TARKIL. LUTH STOOD IN ITS WAY AND SENT IT HOME EMPTY-HANDED.

Here is the thing about Acererak: whatever we tried to cast at him, he cast something back first, every spell, every time. He always had a counterspell ready, and nothing we had ever got past it.

So Ofar jumped.

Off the balcony, out over the lava, at a lich floating in the air; he swung, and he missed.

His plan was to Misty Step back. Acererak saw it coming and counterspelled it. Ofar hung over the lava with nothing under him, and Acererak watched him start to fall.

But that was his counterspell gone.

I had been holding a spell all that while, my finger on it like a trigger: a Chromatic Orb, the biggest I had in me, waiting for exactly that moment.

I let it go.

It hit him, then jumped to the atropal, then back to him, back and forth, five times, six, I lost count, every colour at once, and every time it came back to him there was less of him.

Acererak came apart in the air the way a dream comes apart on waking: his staff, his rings, his robes, everything he had on him went down into the lava and was gone.

And Ofar? Luth's angel, the one he had called down, caught him a hand's breadth above the lava and carried him back up to us like a cat carries a kitten.

HEAR HOW IT WENT. NO SPELL OF OURS GOT PAST HIS COUNTERSPELL. SO I LEAPT FROM THE BALCONY, OUT OVER THE LAVA, MY GLAIVE IN BOTH HANDS, AND MISSED HIM BY A HAND'S BREADTH. I REACHED FOR MISTY STEP. HE TOOK IT FROM ME AND WATCHED ME FALL. THE LAVA'S HEAT ROSE TO MEET ME. THEN OLLI'S ORB OF EVERY COLOUR LEAPT PAST ME INTO THE LICH, AND AT MY BACK LUTH'S ANGEL, ARMOURED, ITS SWORD ABLAZE, CAUGHT ME ERE THE LAVA COULD. MY STROKE FAILED. THEIRS DID NOT.

Orvex says that isn't the end of a lich. Somewhere, far away, is the thing he keeps his soul in, and he grows back around it, slowly, the way a crab grows a new claw.

We decided not to wait for that.

On the south balcony stood an archway of grinning skulls with mist turning inside it, and it led to three places at once.

I'll only write about the third, which went into the Shadowfell.

A tower, standing in a darkness so complete that our lights went into it and didn't come back.

Luth put the darkness out, barely; he says barely, and Luth doesn't exaggerate.

Then up, by a great many stairs. I hate stairs nearly as much as climbing.

At the top of the tower, floating in the air, a big ball of black marble.

His soul. His phylactery.

We didn't try to break it. Scarlett pushed it: off its place and down the tower, all the way down, out through the mist, back into the nursery, and into the ball of nothing that Acererak had left floating there when he came apart. She went into the nothing with it.

It went up, all of it at once, and it hurt every one of us. Scarlett was gone. It was worth it, and I wish it had cost less.

Acererak is finished.

SHE BORE US THROUGH ALL CHULT. AT THE LAST SHE BORE HIS SOUL INTO THE NOTHING, AND WENT WITH IT. NO KNIGHT EVER HAD A BETTER STEED.

Epilogue

In the library down there, among a lot of things that should stay buried, we found a piece of the Rod of Law. Tarkil wanted it more than anything else in the whole tomb. I didn't know why yet. I'm noting it because Orvex made me promise to note it.

And a book called The Chronicle of the Last Reader. Someone called Aruviel is shut inside it now. I wasn't the one reading.

And I still owe a little girl a promise. Her skull is upstairs, in Moa's tomb. I haven't forgotten.

This is the last part of this book. I'm writing it at the very end, at a desk I haven't sat at since I was small. But it doesn't start there.

And then a portal, standing in the mist like a tall mirror. In it, each of us saw our own home.

Ofar's was a village. Luth's was a long black staircase. Mine asked me something, the portal or my own head, I can't tell any more: the temple, or home in Baldur's Gate?

Which home?

I thought about it for a long time. Then I looked at Tarkil, and at Vaeril beside him.

I chose the one I had never seen.

Ofar went to his village. Luth stepped through the mirror, up his staircase, and that is the last any of us saw of him. Tarkil, Vaeril and I went to Kir Sabal.

Kir Sabal

We came out of the mist onto the terrace of the monastery, the three of us, in the middle of the morning ritual.

The monks were dancing in their circle, wings half open in the wind, the way I drew them the first time. And my mother was there. Thalira.

We talked. In Chultan, mostly; mine has got better since the balcony, and she was patient with the rest.

I'm not going to write down what we said. Some things don't go into a book that a paladin, an elf and a warlock have all been reading over my shoulder.

Then Asharra, the elder. She wants Omu. For the owlins: the dead city, the shrines, the palace, all of it. She said it the way other people say they would like a bigger garden.

Then Princess Mwaxanaré, who got her cup at last. The Skull Chalice of Ch'gakare, the one that rose out of the floor under the gears. Tarkil put it into her hands, and she looked at it the way Asharra had looked at Omu.

Two people in Kir Sabal want Omu.

I would like to watch them meet. From very far away.

That evening a Sending came from Syndra Silvane. The woman who hired us in Port Nyanzaru, coughing blood into her handkerchiefs, the first day of all this.

"It's over, Oliver. I'm breathing. The priests say resurrection works again, since tonight. If you want to bring someone back, hurry. Ten thousand gold is waiting."

Owen. Ophelia. Orville. I said the names four times, which is three more than it needs.

I should have gone home that night.

I didn't. Tarkil had one more thing to show me.

The peak

Above Kir Sabal the mountain goes on, higher than the monastery, higher than the clouds, to a flat place at the top with an old stone altar. Tarkil took me up there. I climbed. I hate climbing. I have said so in both books.

He stood at the altar and talked to the sky, the way he did on the wall in Omu. And the sky answered: a storm came up out of nothing, all round the peak.

And then his patron came. One of the Wind Dukes of Aaqa, as big as the mountain we were standing on, made of storm.

Tarkil held up the piece of the Rod of Law from the library. The second piece, he said, as if I ought to know what that meant. The Wind Duke took it. I don't know how something made of weather takes a thing. It did.

In return Tarkil asked for one thing. Not for himself.

My wings.

A sabre took them at Orville's wedding, the night my family died. Nephyr told me once that the elder of his village could bring them back, with a ritual, a bloody one. I thought about the blood for a long time.

In the end it took no blood at all. It took a brother.

Granted.

I have climbed every cliff in Chult with my own two hands and hated every one of them. I am never climbing anything again.

Omu, once more

In the next days we went back to Omu. All the way down into the tomb again, and this time nobody was trying to kill us.

We kept our promises to the spirits. Every god we had carried down there had wanted something, and now there was time to give it to them.

We took the last of the treasures, the ones nobody else is ever going to find.

And I went up to Moa's tomb, to the crystal box with the little girl's skull in it.

I promised her.

So I broke it, as gently as you can break a thing like that. Whatever had been holding her there let go.

Port Nyanzaru

Then Tarkil and I went to Port Nyanzaru, the two of us.

Zhanthi had sent coded news ahead. For a while there were wanted posters of us all over the city, and the reward kept growing. Then they disappeared. Azaka kept quiet for a few days, and then it came out anyway that the villa was us.

Zhanthi and Wakanga O'tamu stood up for us. Zhanthi spread the proof of what Ifan had ordered, the trade and the murders. And Orvex is telling everyone our stories, so now we are heroes, and nobody arrests heroes.

They put on plays now. Ras Nsi. The Soulmonger. Acererak. A weapon shop has renamed itself Ofar – Gefahr, and the gun dealer has a new sign: Olliver Lyonbrooke approved. Two l's. I'm not correcting it.

The last merchant prince has not been replaced yet.

Ord Firebeard rebuilt Camp Vengeance and marched off with Musharib to free the mine. To fight the undead, they say. Musharib finally gets his mine.

The play ends with Acererak getting away. Ours didn't.

Nobody is writing in my margins any more. No blue capitals, no pencil. I keep leaving room for them anyway.

Baldur's Gate

And then home, the two of us.

Pantarius hadn't waited for me to hurry. By the time we came to the house, he had done it already.

Owen. Ophelia. Orville.

All three of them. Alive. Whatever my mother said first, I'm keeping it to myself.

My old room in Baldur's Gate. My toy weapons, lying around the way I left them, under a finger of dust.

The last time I stood in this doorway, I had wings. Now I have them again.

Pantarius looked at me the way he looks at a page with an error on it.

"Oliver? You've changed. What happened?"

I told him. All of it. It took a while.

Then he said: "I found out who ordered it. Ifan Talro'a, a prince in Port Nyanzaru. I suspect that would be of interest."

Ifan. I already knew he was in on it. He's dead. So that's finished, and somehow it doesn't feel finished.

It will have to do. I have other things to feel now.

The others

Ofar told me by Sending. Twenty-five words at a time; it took him several. I'm putting the pieces together here, for him, because he won't.

His village is a couple of days from Baldur's Gate, in the jungle. Two days from my own front door. I am going to visit, and I am not going to walk.

It was too quiet when he came. No noise from the fighting ground. A long, new row of graves. The first person who saw him was a child, who didn't know him and ran away to fetch somebody.

The somebody was his mother, Listazia. She had kept everyone going the whole time he was away.

Zuzuwika came up out of the catacombs, pale. "The souls, they're coming back. You did it." And then: "My sisters deserved to die." Then she sent him off to fetch ingredients for the ritual. Of course she did.

Alfons hugged him, awkwardly. "You look … changed."

The first one they brought back was his sister, Nistali.

He doesn't lose any more of himself at night. All of it came back.

His last Sending ended: I sleep through the night now. You can write that down.

So I have.

Luth went to the Raven Queen.

That is all I know. He stepped through the mirror, and none of us ever heard from him again. No Sending, no letter, nothing. He had given everything away, and I think that included us.

So I can't write his ending. It isn't mine to write. I'm not sure he knows it, either.

I have left the next two pages empty. Not because I had nothing to put there.

One evening I opened the book, and there were words on them already. Not my hand. I don't know whose hand it is. They came between one evening and the next.

I read them once, by the candle. As I read, the words lifted off the paper, a line at a time, and when I looked back for a line it was gone. By the end there was nothing on either page but a few stains.

I don't think they are gone for good. Only gone for me. So I have left the pages to them, and I haven't written a word there since.

Whoever you are, read slowly, and read carefully. I think it is the same for every reader as it was for me:

once, and only once.

The outcome of the elf in this story shall be written down by forces outside of this realm, for there is no one left within it who remembers him whole.

He climbed the polished steps of the palace of the Raven Queen, where the souls of the dead rise like smoke and every memory is kept in its place.

She spoke, and the hall listened.

Thou hast fulfilled thy task, and brought the souls back. That was more than the task of a simple servant. So I take thee into my palace, as my faithful servant. But this asks a sacrifice. Give me thy name, for thou wilt need it no more.

He gave it.

And with the name went all that the name had held: the roads he walked, the faces he loved, the friends who walked those roads beside him. That was the price. It was named before it was paid.

Hereby I name thee Soul Warden. A host is given to thee, and a new task. Countless lost and feeble souls have been set free. Walk with them, and guard them, that they may return.

The host is of the shadar-kai, the Queen's own elves of the Shadowfell. A division of them is his to command, and at their head he walks before the freed dead and leads them home, and does not ask whose they are.

He is in her service now, and shall be for all eternity. There is no end to it, and he asks for none.

What the Queen takes, she keeps. This much the wind has carried here and set down, for as long as it is allowed to stay.

Home

The book is nearly full. I have a list of things still to do: the Wyrmheart Mine, the place where the airship came down, the pirates west of the Aldani, a name in Baldur's Gate called Karala Stola. A village two days away, in the jungle. A mother in Kir Sabal.

Downstairs: Owen, Ophelia, Orville. And Tarkil, at the same table.

My wings are on my back. My brother is downstairs. My family is alive.

I never could lie, so here is the truth:

I'm happy.

— Oliver Lyonbrooke. Thuvien. Both.

variants.title: Owlin · Gunslinger (Fighter / Rogue)
variants.text: The writer of this journal. An owlin raised by a human merchant family in Baldur's Gate; a tinkerer who loves his guns and cannot tell a lie to save his life. He came to Chult because his family can't be brought back while the death curse holds.

variants.title: Owlin · Gunslinger and necromancer (Fighter / Rogue / Wizard)
variants.text: Since one sleepless night in Omu with a skull-bound book, he raises the dead about as well as he shoots. Still a terrible liar, so everyone knows.

variants.name: Oliver Lyonbrooke · Thuvien
variants.title: Owlin · Gunslinger and necromancer
variants.text: His wings are back, given by a Wind Duke because his brother asked. Born Thuvien in Kir Sabal, raised Oliver in Baldur's Gate: both.

variants.name: Vaeril
variants.title: Owlin · Scout from Kir Sabal (so he says)
variants.text: An owlin from Kir Sabal with a green hood, a sword, and a pair of wings that make Oliver jealous. He knocked on a shrine door in Omu and says his friends are prisoners in the palace.

variants.title: Owlin · Warlock, pact of the blade (patron: a Wind Duke of Aaqa)
variants.text: He was never Vaeril. Tarkil of Kir Sabal, warlock of a Wind Duke, and maybe Oliver's brother. He lectures Oliver about honesty.

variants.title: Owlin · Warlock, pact of the blade (patron: a Wind Duke of Aaqa)
variants.text: Tarkil of Kir Sabal, warlock of a Wind Duke, and Oliver's brother: a question asked out loud in Omu said yes. Same height, same feathers.

variants.title: Elf · Cleric of the Raven Queen
variants.text: The dead no longer reach the Raven Queen. Somewhere in the south their souls are caught, and her halls stand silent. She has sent me to find what holds them, and to break it. A raven flies ahead of me. Where it goes, I follow; where it lands, I kneel. My born name I leave unwritten. Shar's priests know it, and hunt it. Let them. All that I am is hers: my breath, my name, my years. She need only ask. — L.

variants.title: Elf · Soul Warden of the Raven Queen
variants.text: Found among my drawings. My hand drew it. I do not know who he was. Below it, in the same hand: the souls are free. I am to lead them home.

variants.title: Human · Explorer
variants.text: A weathered explorer whose ring rimes his hand with frost. Xandala says he is her father.

variants.title: Giant lizard · Ofar's summon
variants.text: Ofar's summoned giant lizard: climbs walls, carries riders, goes hunting at night. Oliver calls him Coco Jambo.

variants.title: Lizard · Stowaway
variants.text: A small, round-eyed lizard found in a devil's mouth in the tomb. Very clever, apparently. He came along. Nobody voted.

variants.name: The rescued owlin
variants.title: Owlin
variants.text: An owlin pulled off a sacrificial altar under the palace. Thin, exhausted and very quiet.

variants.title: Owlin · Scout from Kir Sabal
variants.text: The real Vaeril: a slim scout from Kir Sabal and Tarkil's friend, gentler than the name was made to sound. He goes wherever Tarkil goes.

variants.title: Human (Chultan) · Paladin, Oath of Vengeance
variants.text: I CROSSED THE SEA TO END THE CURSE: TO RAISE MY KIN AND MY FRIENDS FROM THE DEAD, AND TO STAY MINE OWN DEATH. ELEVEN TEETH UPON MY SKIN: ELEVEN TIMES HAVE I DIED, ELEVEN TIMES RETURNED. A HAG'S CURSE RUNS IN MY BLOOD. BY NIGHT, THE RED ANTS. BY MORNING, BLOOD FROM MY NOSE. MY VILLAGE LIES IN THE JUNGLE, TWO DAYS FROM BALDUR'S GATE. MINE OWN CARDS I PAINT. NO OTHER HAND GETS MY FACE RIGHT.
variants.credit: Painted by Ofar himself · gouache on a loose card

variants.title: Human (Chultan) · Paladin, Oath of Vengeance
variants.text: THE GLAIVE OF THE FALLEN KING. AMONG THE DEAD, NA'NBUZO PUT ME TO THE TEST. I HELD FAST TILL HIS LIGHT BURNED IN ME, AND I DREW THE BLADE FROM THE STONE. RED RIBBONS. AN EDGE LIKE A LIVE COAL. A CRY LIKE A WAR HORN. A KING BORE IT ONCE. NOW I BEAR IT, UNTO THE END.
variants.credit: Painted by Ofar himself · gouache on a loose card

variants.text: THE PLATE OF A KNIGHT OF THE YELLOW BANNER. HE DIED DOWN HERE, STILL CLAD IN IT. BY PRAYER I FOUND HIM, AND FROM HIS BONES I TOOK IT. HE DID NOT COME OUT. I SHALL. NOW AT LAST I LOOK WHAT I HAVE ALWAYS SAID I WAS.
